extracted.intended_audience: fiction and creative writers (aspiring and working)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and aesthetic guidance for writing literary fiction: how to approach language, craft, voice, the writer's life, and the transformation of experience into fiction. Emphasizes habits, anti-patterns, and tonal/structural choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer writing as a verb, not an identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Better to think of writing, of what one does as an activity, rather than an identity—to write, I write, we write; to keep the calling a verb rather than a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid thinking of oneself primarily as 'a writer' (an identity or pose), which can lead to a stopped, satisfied, too-healthy complacency. Keep the work active and ongoing to prevent life becoming 'a pornography of wishing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat writing as workmanlike, tenacious skilled labor
rubrics_metrics.description: What writers do is workmanlike: tenacious, skilled labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate steady practice and craft discipline rather than relying solely on inspiration. William Carlos Williams' advice—'Catch an eyeful, catch an earful, and don't drop what you've caught'—supports laborious attention to material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen sentence to sentence; let language lead
rubrics_metrics.description: One must throw all that one is into language... One must listen and proceed, sentence to sentence, hearing what comes next in one's story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose by following the momentum of single sentences; avoid forcing plot or artifice over the organic unfolding of language. This is both a compositional method and a test for whether the writing 'works.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the language sing while it works
rubrics_metrics.description: To make the language sing while it works is a task... to honor the texture of it but also to make it unafraid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance musicality (rhythm, cadence, voice) with clarity and functionality. Language should be both aesthetically pleasing and operationally clear within the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to detail; 'detail, on its own, contains the universe.'
rubrics_metrics.description: The writing will disclose a world; it will be that Heideggerian 'setting–itself-into-work of the truth of what is.' But it will not have lost the detail; detail, on its own, contains the universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize concrete, specific details over abstract grand ideas. Flannery O'Connor's point—fiction focuses on putting 'list slippers on clerks'—is cited as a reminder to ground narratives in lived, particular detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid formula; there is no golden recipe
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no formula, to the life or to the work... Most things literary are stubborn as colds; they resist all formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist seeking universal step-by-step techniques; instead learn craft tools and apply them adaptively. Excessive belief in formulas can stifle the idiosyncratic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for lazy/false-dramatic phrasing (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: How often I've tried to shake from my own storytelling the phrase 'And then suddenly,' as if I could wake up a story with the false drama of those three words. It's usually how I know my writing's going badly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify habitual weak openings or clichés (e.g., 'And then suddenly') as signs of poor drafting. Edit such telltale phrases out; they often indicate forced plot mechanics or lazy exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace paradox and tonal complexity (tragicomedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best art... embraces the very idea of paradox: it sees opposites, antitheses coexisting... tones share space—often queasily, the ironies quivering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow tragedy and comedy, sorrow and pleasure, to coexist in scenes and lines. Use tonal dissonance deliberately (examples: Alice Munro lines, Garrison Keillor) to reflect life’s complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform autobiography into invention—nurture, don't replicate
rubrics_metrics.description: Autobiography can be a useful tool... All the energy that goes into the work... is a kind of autobiographical energy, no matter what one is actually writing about. One must nurture rather than replicate or transcribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personal experience as raw material but rework, paraphrase, and invent rather than transcribing events verbatim. The writer's life should 'creep into' work in characteristic, transformed ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance invention and autobiography (they coax each other)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention and autobiography coax out each other; the pen takes refuge from one in the other, looking for moral dignity and purpose in each, and then flying to the arms of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to oscillating between factual memory and imaginative invention as complementary processes that enrich narrative authenticity and moral focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate an intense, close mode of attention ('doom-eager')
rubrics_metrics.description: Martha Graham speaks of the Icelandic term doom eager to denote that ordeal of isolation, restlessness, caughtness an artist experiences when he or she is sick with an idea. When a writer is doom eager, the writing won't be sludge on the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow periods of restlessness and intense focus where the writer is 'sick' with an idea; this intensity often produces vivid, original work. This is a productive form of obsession rather than mere neurosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep craft and spiritual/ philosophical longing in tension
rubrics_metrics.description: One must think of the craft—that impulse to make an object from the materials lying about, as much as of the spiritual longing, the philosophical sweep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend equally to form (craft, object-making) and the larger human questions that fuel the work; neither aspect should wholly dominate the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use voice that feels like a song or confiding letter
rubrics_metrics.description: I often think... that that is what I tried to find later in literature: the feeling of a song; the friendly, confiding voice of a letter but the cadence and feeling of a song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a close, intimate narrative voice—music-like cadence combined with the confiding immediacy of a letter—to engage readers emotionally and rhythmically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect miscellanea—be a magpie for material
rubrics_metrics.description: I had become a magpie, collecting shiny objects... I had begun a secret life. A secret harvest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather stray details, objects, images, and fragments (notes, clipped phrases, ephemera). These collections supply the raw materials that can be recombined into richer fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to disclose a world and give readers new experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: The writing will disclose a world; it will give readers—and the writer...—an experience they've never had before, or perhaps a little and at last the words for an experience they have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for narrative revelation: your prose should open onto a recognizable but newly-seen world, providing readers with novel perceptions or emotional recognitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical life arrangement supports writing
rubrics_metrics.description: One should also live with someone who can cook and who will both be with one and leave one alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider practical domestic arrangements that allow sustained focus: companionship that supports both presence and solitude, and basic practical help (meals, household stability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept marginality and shamelessness as part of artistic life
rubrics_metrics.description: Certainly so much of art originates and locates itself within the margins—that is, the contours—of the human self, as a form of locating and defining that self. And certainly art, and the life of the artist, requires a goodly amount of shamelessness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to inhabit margins, eccentricity, and to act without excessive shame in service of creating distinctive work. Marginal perspectives can produce original aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of excessive production and social offense
rubrics_metrics.description: But then excessive literary production, George Eliot reminds us, is a social offense. As far as language goes we have to live contentedly, and discontentedly, with our own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid producing work solely to flood the market or to satiate output quotas; focus on quality and the limits of what language can bear. Respect language's limits while pushing them thoughtfully.
